624.title: Neither coming nor going
624.hook: a sphere where there is no earth, water, fire or wind, no coming or going
624.howItsDone: This passage is often read in Theravada teaching on nibbana, and some meditation teachers cite it when explaining that the goal is not a meditative state or a heavenly place.

segments.voice: Yesterday: four words that begin with un, and your line, because there is, an escape is known. Did you remember it when something changed? Today, the saying that opens the same chapter. Day six hundred twenty-four.
screen: `BECAUSE THERE IS, AN ESCAPE IS KNOWN.`

segments.voice: Try to describe silence without mentioning sound. Or darkness without mentioning light. It's almost impossible; we describe things by what's in them. The first discourse of the Udana's last chapter takes on an even harder job. The Buddha is instructing the monks about nibbana, and the text says they listen with their whole minds, paying close attention, ears open. What he gives them is not a description. It's a list of everything that isn't there. Today: neither coming nor going.
screen: `DESCRIBE SILENCE WITHOUT SOUND.` → `THE MONKS LISTEN CLOSELY.` → `A LIST OF WHAT ISN'T THERE.`

segments.voice: There is, monks, that sphere, he says, where there is no earth, no water, no fire, no wind. Those four elements were the ancient way of naming everything solid, liquid, hot and moving: everything physical. None of it there. Then he goes further. Not the sphere of infinite space, not infinite consciousness, not nothingness, not neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Those are the four formless states the texts describe, very subtle places a meditating mind can reach. Not those either. Not this world, not another world, not sun, not moon. There, he says, there is no coming, no going, no staying, no passing away, no arising. It has no support, no movement, no basis. This, just this, is the end of dukkha. Notice what's been done. Yesterday's saying named the unborn. Today's empties out every place you might look for it, from the ground under your feet to the highest heaven of the mind. Even the formless states are set aside. And then, after all those nots, one word of yes: this is the end of suffering. Theravada teachers read the passage as describing nibbana, which isn't a place in the ordinary sense, even though the text calls it a sphere.
screen: `NO EARTH, WATER, FIRE, WIND.` · `NOT EVEN THE FORMLESS STATES.` · `NO COMING, NO GOING, NO STAYING.` · `THIS, JUST THIS.` · then, large: `THE END OF DUKKHA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen the way the monks listened. Settle. Give the listening your whole mind, ears open. A sound arrives; follow it until it ends. Another arrives; follow that one too. Notice that each sound has a coming and a going, and that between sounds there's a gap. Don't fill the gap with a thought. Just keep listening, without reaching for anything. The bell holds the time.
Ayatana, a sphere or base. The Udana's words for nibbana: no earth, water, fire or wind; no coming, going or staying; just this, the end of dukkha. Today's word.
Your line: the end of dukkha. Today, when you're rushing between places, stop for one breath and listen the way the monks did, with your whole mind. Day six hundred twenty-four.

options: but there are the formless states of meditation.

fork.reveal: he sets aside even the subtlest states, and this world and the next. then: this, just this, is the end of dukkha.

trapdoor: what you thought: nirvana is a peaceful place you go to.
what it means: the Udana describes it by what it isn't: no elements, no states, no coming, going or staying; just the end of dukkha.
what a scholar hears: Udana 8.1 lists the four elements, the four formless spheres, this world and the next and sun and moon, then ends 'esevanto dukkhassa': this is the end of dukkha.

625.title: No blame to Cunda
625.hook: the smith's meal, and the Buddha's care that he not be blamed
625.carry: for one who gives, merit grows
625.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often tell of Cunda's meal as an example of the Buddha's compassion at the end of his life, and tradition identifies the meal before the awakening as Sujata's offering of milk-rice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: no earth, no water, no coming or going, and your line, the end of dukkha. Did you find one still breath while rushing? Today, from the same chapter, a very human worry. Day six hundred twenty-five.

A cook makes dinner for a guest she admires. That night the guest gets sick. Even if the food had nothing to do with it, the cook lies awake. Was it the fish? Should I have known? And if the guest died, that question could follow her for years. In the first year of this path, on day eighty-one, you heard about Cunda, the smith's son at Pava, who served the Buddha his last meal. The Udana tells the same story in its eighth chapter, and it keeps a detail that's easy to pass over: what the Buddha did about Cunda's feelings, while he himself was dying. Today: no blame to Cunda.
screen: `DINNER, THEN SICKNESS.` → `WAS IT THE FISH?` → `CUNDA, THE SMITH'S SON.`

segments.voice: Cunda invites the Buddha and the monks for a meal, and among the dishes is one called sukaramaddava. Nobody today knows for certain what it was. Its name has the word for pig in it. The commentaries take it as tender pork; other readers have taken it as a kind of mushroom, or a herbal preparation. The text doesn't say. The Buddha tells Cunda to serve that dish to him alone, and to bury what's left, since no one else could digest it. After the meal, a severe illness comes on him, with sharp pains. He bears it, mindful, and travels on toward Kusinara. And on the road, sick and near the end, he thinks of Cunda. Someone, he tells Ananda, might make Cunda feel remorse: it's your loss, Cunda, that the Teacher passed away after eating your food. So go and dispel it. Tell him this, from me: two offerings of food bring equal and great fruit, more than any others. The meal after which the Teacher awoke, and the meal after which he passes into final release. Cunda's act was good; it brings long life, beauty, happiness and honor. Look at the care in that. The Buddha is dying, and he spends some of his last strength protecting a man from guilt that wasn't his. The verse says it plainly: for one who gives, merit grows.
screen: `A DISH NO ONE CAN NAME FOR SURE.` · `SERVE IT TO ME ALONE.` · `GO AND DISPEL HIS REMORSE.` · `TWO MEALS OF EQUAL FRUIT.` · then, large: `NO BLAME TO CUNDA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: protect someone's feelings. Sit and settle. Think of someone who might be blaming themselves for something that isn't really their fault: a parent, a coworker, a friend after a bad day, maybe even you. Picture them. Notice the weight they're carrying. Then think of one thing you could say, simply and truly, that would lift some of it, the way the Buddha sent word to Cunda. Hold that sentence, ready. The bell holds the time.
Cunda. The smith's son whose meal the Buddha ate before he died; the Buddha sent Ananda to tell him his offering was among the two greatest. Today's word.
Your line: for one who gives, merit grows. Today, say the sentence you found to the person carrying blame that isn't theirs. Day six hundred twenty-five.

what it means: the story's weight is on his care: dying, he made sure the giver wasn't blamed.

626.title: Thus it was said
626.hook: 112 short teachings, remembered by the laywoman Khujjuttara, a servant of the queen
626.carry: she came back with something better
626.howItsDone: The Itivuttaka is part of the Khuddaka Nikaya and is read and taught in Theravada communities; Khujjuttara is honored as a model of the learned lay disciple.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the smith's meal, and your line, for one who gives, merit grows. Did you lift someone's blame off them? The Udana is behind us. Today, the third of the short books. Day six hundred twenty-six.

In the city of Kosambi, the story goes, Queen Samavati gives her servant money every day to buy flowers. And every day the servant, a woman named Khujjuttara, keeps some of the money for herself. Then one day she hears the Buddha teach, and she comes home with the full amount, and all the flowers it buys. The queen notices. Khujjuttara confesses. And then the queen asks her for something far more valuable than flowers. Today: the Itivuttaka, thus it was said.
screen: `MONEY FOR FLOWERS.` → `ONE DAY, THE FULL AMOUNT.` → `SOMETHING MORE VALUABLE.`

segments.voice: The queen and her women, the commentary says, couldn't leave the palace to hear the Buddha. So they asked Khujjuttara to go for them, and to bring the teaching home. She went, she listened, and she came back and taught them, word for word, what she'd heard. The collection that tradition says grew from her memory is the Itivuttaka. Its name means thus it was said. Every one of its 112 short discourses opens with the same humble line: this was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant, so I heard. Not I say. Not the Buddha says. This was said, and I heard it. It's the voice of someone passing on what they were given, carefully, without adding. The teachings are arranged by number: a section of ones, of twos, of threes, of fours. Each is short: a few lines of prose, then verse that says it again. Khujjuttara's name means the hunchbacked Uttara, and she was a servant. Yet in the canon's list of outstanding disciples, she is named foremost among laywomen who had heard much. In the tradition's telling, the person who kept these teachings wasn't a monk or a scholar or a queen. She was the woman sent to buy flowers, who came back with something better.
screen: `THE QUEEN COULDN'T GO.` · `SHE BROUGHT IT HOME, WORD FOR WORD.` · `THIS WAS SAID, SO I HEARD.` · `FOREMOST OF THE LEARNED.` · then, large: `THUS IT WAS SAID.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one, the way Khujjuttara carried them. Before that, sit and settle. Think of one good thing someone taught you, a sentence, a habit, a way of seeing, that has stayed with you. Who said it? Let their face come to mind. Notice that you're a link in a chain, holding something that was handed to you. Then, after the bell, read one short teaching from the Itivuttaka, and see if you can carry it home. The bell holds the time.
Itivuttaka. Thus it was said: 112 short teachings, each opening with this was said, so I heard, kept, tradition says, by the servant Khujjuttara. Today's word.
Your line: she came back with something better. Today, pass on one good thing someone once told you, and say whose words they were. Day six hundred twenty-six.

627.title: Just one thing
627.hook: abandon greed, just that one thing, and I guarantee the fruit
627.carry: pull it up by the root
627.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often name greed, hatred and delusion as the three roots of unwholesome action, and some practitioners work with one of them at a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Khujjuttara and the flower money, and your line, she came back with something better. Did you pass on something you were once told? Today, the very first teaching in her book. Day six hundred twenty-seven.

Self-help shelves are full of lists. Seven habits. Twelve rules. Thirty days to a better you. Lists are useful, and the Buddhist texts love them too: four truths, eight factors, five hindrances. But sometimes a list is a way of putting things off; there's always one more item to read about before starting. The Itivuttaka opens with no list at all. Its section of ones begins with a single thing, and an unusual promise. The Buddha doesn't say try this. He says: I guarantee it. Today: just one thing.
screen: `SEVEN HABITS, TWELVE RULES.` → `A LIST CAN BE A DELAY.` → `ONE THING, AND A GUARANTEE.`

segments.voice: Here is the first teaching of the book, after the opening line, this was said by the Blessed One, so I heard. Abandon one thing, monks, and I am your guarantee of non-return. What one thing? Greed. Non-return is a technical term. In the early texts, it's the third of four stages of awakening: someone who has gone so far that they won't be reborn in this world of the senses again. So the promise is enormous. And the condition is one thing. The verse that follows explains: driven by greed, beings go to a bad destination; seeing greed rightly, those who understand let it go, and having let it go, they don't come back to this world. Then the very next teachings say the same, one at a time. Abandon one thing: hatred. Then: delusion. Then anger, then contempt, then conceit. Each one, alone, with the same guarantee. Why would one be enough? The text doesn't say. One way teachers explain it: these aren't six separate weeds; pull one up by the root, really by the root, and the others turn out to grow from the same soil. Notice the word guarantee, too. The Pali word, patibhoga, means a guarantor, someone who stands surety. In the text, the Buddha puts his own word behind the promise.
screen: `ABANDON ONE THING: GREED.` · `NON-RETURN, THE THIRD STAGE.` · `HATRED, DELUSION, ANGER, CONCEIT.` · `I STAND AS YOUR GUARANTEE.` · then, large: `JUST ONE THING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: abandon one small thing. Sit and settle. Ask, where does a little greed show up in my day? A second helping you don't want. Checking a price again. Wanting the last word. Choose just one, and make it small. Picture the moment it usually happens, and picture yourself letting it go: hand open, breath out. Not forever. Just today. The bell holds the time.
Lobha, greed. The opening of the Itivuttaka: abandon this, just that, and the Buddha stands as your guarantee. Today's word.
Your line: pull it up by the root. Today, don't fix everything. Let go of the one small grab you chose, once, and notice what's left. Day six hundred twenty-seven.

screen: `DAY 627 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SHARE EVEN THE LAST BITE.`

628.title: Share even the last bite
628.hook: if beings knew the result of giving, they would not eat without sharing
628.howItsDone: In many Buddhist homes a portion of food is set aside or offered before eating, and giving food to monks, neighbors and those in need is among the most common daily acts of generosity.

segments.voice: Yesterday: abandon greed, just that, and your line, pull it up by the root. Did you let go of one small grab? Today, the same book shows what the open hand does next. Day six hundred twenty-eight.

Two kids, one cookie left. Watch what happens. Usually it's a negotiation: who had more, who's bigger, who asked first. And sometimes, rarely, one of them just breaks it and hands over half without being asked. Grown-ups do the same math with bigger things. In the first year of this path, on day one hundred thirty-four, you met this teaching from the Itivuttaka: if people knew, they'd share. Today we read it again, closer, and listen for three small words in the middle of it: as I know. Today: share even the last bite.
screen: `TWO KIDS, ONE COOKIE.` → `WHO HAD MORE?` → `THREE SMALL WORDS: AS I KNOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the teaching. If beings knew, as I know, the result of giving and sharing, they would not eat without having given, and the stain of stinginess would not take hold of their minds. Even if it were their last bite, their last mouthful, they would not eat without sharing it, if there were someone to receive it. But because beings don't know, as I know, the result of giving and sharing, they eat without having given, and the stain of stinginess takes hold of their minds. Now the phrase: as I know. The Buddha isn't saying be nicer. He's saying the problem is not knowing. If you could really see what giving does, to the receiver and to the giver, you wouldn't need to be told; you'd just do it, the way you'd step out of the rain. Stinginess, in this teaching, is a kind of blindness, and the word for it is a stain, something that clouds the mind. Notice too the small realism at the end: if there were someone to receive it. The teaching isn't asking anyone to throw food away to prove a point. It's about the moment when there's someone in front of you. And notice the scale. Not a fortune. A mouthful. The last bite is about as small as a gift can be. That's the point. Even there, the hand can open.
screen: `IF BEINGS KNEW, AS I KNOW.` · `THE STAIN OF STINGINESS.` · `EVEN THE LAST MOUTHFUL.` · `IF THERE WERE SOMEONE TO RECEIVE.` · then, large: `SHARE EVEN THE LAST BITE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share food today. First, sit and settle. Remember a time someone shared food with you when they didn't have much: a grandparent, a stranger, a friend splitting a sandwich. Feel what it did to you then. Let it warm the chest. Now think ahead to your next meal. Who will be near you? Picture yourself offering them something from your plate, or bringing an extra for someone. Just picture it, and enjoy it. The bell holds the time.
Samvibhaga, sharing. Itivuttaka 26: if beings knew, as the Buddha knows, the result of giving, they'd share even their last mouthful. Today's word.
Your line: notice who it feeds. Today, share some food with someone, even just a bite. Day six hundred twenty-eight.

629.title: The moon outshines
629.hook: all merit-making is not worth a sixteenth part of metta, as starlight to moonlight
629.howItsDone: Metta practice is taught in Theravada communities and in other Buddhist schools; practitioners often begin with someone easy to love and widen the wish of goodwill step by step to all beings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: if beings knew, as I know, and your line, notice who it feeds. Did someone get a bite of your lunch? Today, the very next teaching in the book, and it sets something above even generosity. Day six hundred twenty-nine.

Go outside on a clear night far from city lights and the stars are astonishing, the whole sky crowded. Then the full moon rises. And as it climbs, the fainter stars fade out. They're all still there. The moon just outshines them. The Itivuttaka uses that exact sight. Yesterday it praised giving, generously, as something people would never skip if they understood it. Today, right after, it says there's something brighter still. Today: the moon outshines.
screen: `A SKY CROWDED WITH STARS.` → `THEN THE FULL MOON RISES.` → `SOMETHING BRIGHTER STILL.`

segments.voice: Whatever grounds there are for making merit, the Buddha says, giving, offerings, good works of every kind, all of them together are not worth a sixteenth part of the mind's release through metta, loving-kindness. Metta outshines them; it shines and glows and blazes. Then three pictures. As the light of all the stars together is not worth a sixteenth part of the moon's light. As in the last month of the rainy season, in autumn, when the sky is clear, the sun rising into the sky drives away all the darkness. As at the end of the night, the morning star shines and glows and blazes. So metta outshines all merit-making. Not worth a sixteenth part: a tiny fraction. Notice what's being compared. Giving is good; yesterday's teaching made that clear, and nothing here takes it back. But giving is something you do. Metta, here, is something you become: a mind that wishes well to every being, without measure. One way to hear it: the gift is one star, and the heart it comes from is the moon. And look at the verse at the end. One who develops metta, it says, has their fetters wear thin. Even toward one being, loving-kindness makes a person good. Toward all beings, with a kind heart, the noble one makes abundant merit.
screen: `NOT A SIXTEENTH PART OF METTA.` · `THE STARS AND THE MOON.` · `THE AUTUMN SUN, THE MORNING STAR.` · `THE GIFT AND THE HEART IT COMES FROM.` · then, large: `THE MOON OUTSHINES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: metta. Two minutes now, and if you like, five more later. Sit and settle. Start with one being who is easy to love, a child, a friend, a pet. Feel goodwill toward them: may you be well, may you be happy. Then let it widen: the people in this building, this street, this city. Then wider. Don't force it. The moon doesn't strain to shine. When the mind wanders, come back to that first easy face, and begin again. The bell holds the time.
Metta, loving-kindness. Itivuttaka 27: all merit-making together is not worth a sixteenth part of this, as starlight is to the moon. Today's word.
Your line: let goodwill rise first. Today, before one kind act, pause, so the deed comes from the moon, not just the star. Day six hundred twenty-nine.

630.title: Two bright guardians
630.hook: conscience and concern for consequences protect the world
630.howItsDone: Theravada teachers often call hiri and ottappa the guardians of the world (lokapala dhamma), and they are counted among the wholesome qualities in Abhidhamma lists and in many Buddhist teachings on ethics.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the stars fading as the moon rose, and your line, let goodwill rise first. Did goodwill come before one kind act? Today closes a week, with two quiet protectors. Day six hundred thirty.

A driver backs out in an empty parking lot and scrapes a parked car. Nobody saw. There's no camera. She could drive away. And yet something stops her hand on the gear shift. Maybe it's a feeling: I'm not someone who does that. Maybe it's a thought: what happens to them, and to me, if I do? There's no police officer in that moment. Something inside is keeping watch. The Itivuttaka names two of those inner guards, and calls them bright. Today: two bright guardians.
screen: `A SCRAPE IN THE PARKING LOT.` → `NOBODY SAW.` → `SOMETHING INSIDE KEEPS WATCH.`

segments.voice: Two bright qualities, the Buddha says, protect the world. Which two? Hiri and ottappa. They're hard to translate. Hiri is often rendered moral shame or conscience: the inward sense that this act is beneath me. Ottappa is moral dread or concern for consequences: the outward sense of what this act would do, and how it would look to the wise. One looks in, one looks out. If these two did not protect the world, the text says, people would no longer honor the bonds that hold families and communities together, not mother, not aunt, not a teacher's wife, and the world would fall into confusion. But because these two bright qualities guard the world, those bonds are recognized. That's the whole teaching. Notice the word bright. In the early texts, sukka, bright, is used for wholesome qualities, as dark is for unwholesome ones. These aren't the gnawing, sticky guilt that keeps a person up at night. Hiri and ottappa, as teachers often explain them, look forward, and stop the hand before the harm. And notice the scale: the world. Not just my peace of mind. Look back at the week. Neither coming nor going. No blame to Cunda. Thus it was said. Just one thing. Share even the last bite. The moon outshines. Most of them turned toward other people: a smith, a servant, a last bite, a wish for every being. Today's two guardians keep watch over how we treat them.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to conscience gently. Sit and settle. Think of a moment this week when something in you said, don't. Maybe you listened. Maybe you didn't. Either way, recall the voice itself. Notice it wasn't cruel. It was just clear. Thank it, quietly. If there's an old guilt that keeps gnawing, notice the difference between that and this bright guard, and let the guilt soften. Rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Hiri, conscience or moral shame. Paired with ottappa, concern for consequences, the two qualities the Itivuttaka says protect the world. Today's word.
Your line: listen to the small don't. Today, when you feel that inner pause rise up, listen to it for one breath before you decide. Day six hundred thirty.
